title: PPOL 5203 - Data Science I: Foundations
text:
Why data visualization?

Visualization matters! A figure is almost always more compelling than a table or a crosstab
This course covers the basics; you’ll have a full semester of Data Visualization later in the program
Focus of today:

Grammar of graphics and plotnine (a ggplot2 implementation in Python)
A brief tour of the native Python libraries matplotlib and seaborn

text:
Quiz: what do you see?




How many variables (data) are mapped in this graph?
How are these variables (non-constant) represented in the figure?
What are the non-data (constant) related elements presented in the graph?

title: PPOL 5203 - Data Science I: Foundations
text:
Aesthetics

All data visualizations map data values into quantifiable features of the resulting graphic. We refer to these features as aesthetics.
— Fundamentals of Data Visualization, Claus Wilke

Aesthetics: visual mappings that connect data variables to visual attributes of graphical elements

title: PPOL 5203 - Data Science I: Foundations
text:
Cartesian coordinates system: 2d
Humans can very easily understand information in two dimensions; most of our work will consist of mapping data onto an X and a Y axis

title: PPOL 5203 - Data Science I: Foundations
section: Adding a 3rd, 4th, 5th variable in a 2d space
text:
Adding a 3rd, 4th, 5th variable in a 2d space
We often want to map more variables into the graph. For example, we might want to:

Distinguish discrete items or groups that don’t have an intrinsic order
Highlight values that pass a certain threshold
Represent a sequential/continuous data value

To add these to a 2d graph, we map them to new aesthetics (color, shape, size, alpha…)

title: PPOL 5203 - Data Science I: Foundations
text:
Grammar of graphics
Grammar: the set of structural rules that dictate how words in a language can be combined to form meaningful sentences
Grammar of graphics: brings a similar effort to establish structural rules for data visualizations — first developed in Leland Wilkinson’s book The Grammar of Graphics
Implementation:

ggplot2 in R (developed by Hadley Wickham)
plotnine in Python — an emulator of ggplot2

Native Python libraries (matplotlib, seaborn) don’t use this framework, but we’ll focus on plotnine because it enforces a systematic, structured approach to building a wide variety of visualizations

title: PPOL 5203 - Data Science I: Foundations
section: Major components of the grammar of graphics
text:
Major components of the grammar of graphics
plotnine/ggplot2 graphs have three key steps:

Data step: the raw data you want to plot
Geometries geom_ step: the geometric shapes that represent the data
Aesthetics aes() step: aesthetics of the geometric/statistical objects — position, color, size, shape, transparency

title: PPOL 5203 - Data Science I: Foundations
section: Additional components of the grammar of graphics
text:
Additional components of the grammar of graphics

Facets: create subplots based on a specific variable
Annotations: labels, titles, subtitles, captions
Coordinates & scales: adjust the aesthetics you’re mapping (colors, size, alpha, scale of x/y coordinates)
Theme: control finer presentation details — font size, background color, grid line styles, etc.

# step 3: aesthetics as a variable

title: PPOL 5203 - Data Science I: Foundations
text:
Putting it all together

# step 1: data
(ggplot(data=gapminder) +

# step 2: geom
 geom_point(
     aes(x="lngdpPercap", y="lifeExp", color="continent"),
        alpha=.2, size=3) +

# step scale: manually edit the aesthetic's values
scale_color_manual(values = ["blue","steelblue","black","gold","pink"],
                  name="Continent") +

# step theme: change the overall look of the graph
theme_minimal(base_size=16) +

# step facet: break the graph into subplots
facet_wrap("continent", scales="free") +

# step labels: edit the labels of the graph
labs(x="Log GDP Per Capita", y="Life Expectancy",
     title="Gdp vs Life Expectancy Across the World")
)

What is Git?

Set of command line tools for version control (aka avoid finalfinal, finalrealthistime, etc.)
``Distributed,’’ or means that files/code, rather than only stored one place centrally, can be stored on all collaborators’ machines

title: PPOL 5203 - Data Science I: Foundations
text:
What is GitHub?

Web-based repository for code that utilizes version control system (VCS) for tracking changes
Has additional features useful for collaboration, some of which we’ll review today (repos; issues; push/pulling recent changes) and others of which we’ll review as the course progresses (branches; pull requests)
Why GitHub rather than Dropbox/Google Drive?

Explicit features that help with simultaneous editing of the same file
Public-facing record, or a portfolio of code/work (if you make it public)
Ways to comment on and have discussions about code specifically through the interface

title: PPOL 5203 - Data Science I: Foundations
text:
For these files and directories

File names should be meaningful
DO NOT USE SPACES. Use snake case (_) style for you files and code
Also allows you to avoid capitalization (FileName → file_name)




data analysis 2.py → data_analysis_2.py





model_analysis.py → model_analysis_het_treatment_effects_main_paper.py

title: PPOL 5203 - Data Science I: Foundations
text:
Ingredients of a repo: data?
Depending on the context, you may store data, but

GitHub has file size limits (though can pay to override these)
Sensitive data should generally not be put in a repo, even if the repo is private since employees at the company have access to private repo content
Instead, read data directly from its source or have download instructions

text:

Can assign to specific collaborators or leave as a “note to self” to look back at something
Can use checklist features
Can include code excerpts
Easy to link to a specific commit (change to code)
Need to be logged into GitHub to write

title: PPOL 5203 - Data Science I: Foundations
text:
General steps in workflow

Either create a repository locally and link to GitHub OR create a repository on GitHub and clone
Make changes to code or other files

text:
Broadcasting

Broadcasting makes it possible for operations to be performed on arrays of mismatched shapes.
Broadcasting describes how numpy treats arrays with different shapes during arithmetic operations.
Subject to certain constraints, the smaller array is “broadcast” across the larger array so that they have compatible shapes.

title: PPOL 5203 - Data Science I: Foundations
text:
Example: adding to an array

A 5 x 1 array

\[
\begin{bmatrix} 1\\2\\3\\4\\5\end{bmatrix}
\] \[
\begin{bmatrix} 1\\2\\3\\4\\5\end{bmatrix} + 5
\]

title: PPOL 5203 - Data Science I: Foundations
text:
Example: adding to an array
Broadcasting “pads” the array of 5 (which is shape = 1,1), and extends it so that it has similar dimension to the larger array in which the computation is being performed.
\[
\begin{bmatrix} 1\\2\\3\\4\\5\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 5\\\color{lightgrey}{5}\\\color{lightgrey}{5}\\\color{lightgrey}{5}\\\color{lightgrey}{5}\end{bmatrix}
\]
\[
\begin{bmatrix} 1 + 5\\2 + 5\\3 + 5\\4 + 5\\5 + 5\end{bmatrix}
\]
\[
\begin{bmatrix} 6\\7\\8\\9\\10\end{bmatrix}
\]

title: PPOL 5203 - Data Science I: Foundations
text:
Split step within pandas: groupby

The groupby() method in pandas splits your dataset in smaller parts. It generates an iterable where each group is broken up into a tuple (group,data).
The output of a groupby method is a flexible abstraction: although more complicated things are happening under the hood, in many ways, it can be treated as a collection of DataFrames. And as we learned, any collector can be iterated over!

Quick tutorial for RStudio
This is what RStudio looks like when you open it for the first time.









Top left pane (input/script)
This is your code editor. Here you enter code in any file type (.py, .r, .qmd) you are working on. If not working with notebooks, this is just gonna be a plain text file but with a extension that run the commands.
For example, enter 2 + 2 in your script and run a line of code by pressing command + enter (Mac) or Ctrl + enter (PC). This is a huge advantage of Rstudio over Jupyter. You can run your code line by line, instead of running the entire cell.
Bottom left pane (output/console)
This is the console. It is pretty much like when you open Python/R from the Command line.
In the console, the prompt > looks like a greater than symbol. If your prompt begins to look like a + symbol by mistake, simply click in your console and press the esc key on your keyboard as many times as necessary to return to the prompt.
Rstudio uses + when code is broken up across multiple lines and is still expecting more code. A line of code does not usually end until Rstudio finds an appropriate stop parameter or punctuation that completes some code such as a closed round parenthesis ), square bracket ], curly brace }, or quotation mark '.
If the output in your console gets too messy, you can clear it by pressing control + l on both Mac and PC. This will not erase any saved data - it will simply make your console easier to read.
Top right pane (global environment)
This is your environment pane. All objects you create will be displayed here.
Bottom right pane (files, plots, packages, and help)
Here you find useful tabs for navigating your file system, displaying plots, installing packages, and viewing help pages. Press the control key and a number (1 through 9) on your keyboard to shortcut between these panes and tabs.

Object-Oriented Programming: What are these classes?


Instantiation: When we create a object, we are creating an instance of this class.
Inheritance: Every time we create an object, the objects inherits a class.

A class is a blueprint holding of the properties of a particular data structure.
An instance is a realization of a particular class. This instance inherits the characteristics of its class.

Components: Classes have two major components:

Attributes: these are constant features, data, a characteristic of the broader class. For instance, many objects have some sort of length attribute.
Methods: these are actions, behaviors of this class. For instance, you might have a mean or median method you can apply to an object.

Polymorphism: Both attributes and methods are accessed through . function, conditional on the class

Three general routes to acquiring data


Exists already
csv or excel data like we’ve been working with for problem sets

API
Use code (rather than point and click) to create data or flat files; most relevant for “high-velocity” data that changes frequently (e.g., social media posts; job postings)

Scraping

Why go through the effort to use data that doesn’t exist already?

Guarantees that you’re working with original data \(\implies\) research question is likely novel
Study rapidly changing phenomena missed in static flat files
Rule of thumb: if you can use an API to access a dataset, that’s where you will want to go — APIs are developed by the data owners, so they’re often more secure, practical, and organized than scraping

title: PPOL 5203 - Data Science I: Foundations
text:
Terminology

API: application programming interface; a way to ask an app or website for something and get something in return
Call the API: sending a request for something to the API
Response: a message back telling us whether we got something back or whether the call returned an error
JSON: if we get something back, it’s often stored in json format — a text string with a structure similar to the data structure of a dictionary; pretty easy to convert to a pandas DataFrame
Wrapper: a language-specific module or package that simplifies calling an API from that language (e.g., census is a Python wrapper for the Census Bureau’s API)

title: PPOL 5203 - Data Science I: Foundations
text:
Why Census data?

The American Community Survey (ACS) is the Census Bureau’s ongoing survey of ~3.5 million addresses per year; it’s the main source of detailed data on income, poverty, housing, education, language, and more
Available for many geographies: nation, states, counties, census tracts, and smaller
Used to allocate federal funding, draw districts, and in countless policy evaluations — and it’s a very common “right-hand side” dataset to merge onto your own data
Two common versions:

ACS 1-year: more current, but only for areas with 65,000+ people
ACS 5-year: pooled over five years; available down to small geographies like tracts

title: PPOL 5203 - Data Science I: Foundations
section: The Census API and the census wrapper
text:
The Census API and the census wrapper

API: https://api.census.gov — requires a free API key
Wrapper: the census package (developed by DataMade)
Recall our earlier steps for NAEP and Yelp:

Set up credentials (where relevant)
Constructed a query based on the API documentation
Used requests.get(query) to call the API
Got a response
Extracted the content of the response and turned it into usable data

The wrapper simplifies steps 2-5: instead of a long query string, we call methods that name the dataset and geography we want, and get back data that’s easy to convert to a DataFrame
Downside: we need to learn the wrapper’s methods (but this is often easier than constructing queries ourselves)

Step 1: acquire and store credentials

Request a key here: https://api.census.gov/data/key_signup.html — it arrives by email; you need to click the link in the email to activate it
Add it to your yaml credentials file, e.g.:

census_api:
  api_key: 'YOUR_KEY_HERE'

Load it the same way as the Yelp key:

title: PPOL 5203 - Data Science I: Foundations
text:
What is scraping?
Scraping: automatically collecting data available on websites. In theory, you could collect website data by hand — but in a world of abundant data, this is rarely feasible
Examples of websites that have been scraped for research:

Electoral data from many different countries
Composition of elites around the world
Wikipedia
Political manifestos
Fact-checking news
Property prices from Zillow

Scraping can be summarized as:

Leveraging the structure of a website to grab its contents
Using a programming environment (such as R, Python, Java, etc.) to systematically extract that content
Accomplishing the above in an “unobtrusive” and legal way

title: PPOL 5203 - Data Science I: Foundations
text:
Ethical challenges with scraping
Web scraping is legal as long as the scraped data is publicly available and the scraping activity does not harm the website being scraped — two hugely relevant conditions

Each call to a web server takes time, server cycles, and memory; massive automated requests can overload a site, taking it offline or causing the site administrator to ban your IP (see denial-of-service attack)
Best practice: only collect public information (e.g., public posts are OK; content from private groups where members expect privacy is not)

Good practices for scraping:

Respect robots.txt
Don’t hit servers too often; slow your code down to the speed a human would browse
Find trusted source sites
Avoid scraping during peak hours
Use data responsibly

Step 4: build a scraper
Once your scraper works for a single case, generalize it by creating a function — and build in good practices that imitate human behavior

def cnn_scraper(url=None):
    '''
    this function scrapes relevant content from the cnn website
    input: str, url from cnn
    '''
    # get access to the website
    page = requests.get(url)
    # create a bs object
    soup = BeautifulSoup(page.content, 'html.parser')
    # check if you got a connection
    if page.status_code == 200:
        # parse text
        cnn_par = soup.select(".vossi-paragraph_elevate")
        story_content = [i.get_text() for i in cnn_par]
        story_text = "\n".join([i.strip() for i in story_content])
        # parse title
        story_title = soup.select("#maincontent")[0].get_text()
        # story date
        story_date = soup.select(".vossi-timestamp_elevate")[0].get_text()
        # nest all in a dictionary
        entry = {"url": url, "story_title": story_title.strip(),
                 "story_date": story_date.strip(), "text": story_text}
        return entry
